The uptime command reported that this machine has been up for 21 days and 15 hours, with 2 users logged in, and load averages of 6.95, 6.26, and 6.16. Those three numbers are the average number of processes that were runnable or waiting on disk over the last 1, 5, and 15 minutes. A value near 7 means roughly seven tasks were competing for CPU or I/O at a time, which is moderate to busy depending on how many cores the host has. The three figures are close together and slightly higher in the one-minute window, so the load is steady rather than a short spike that already faded.

A high load average on a build server means jobs are queued behind CPU or disk instead of finishing as soon as they start. Compiles, tests, and package installs then take longer, and a queue of CI jobs can back up even if each individual build is healthy. If the load stays well above the core count for the 15-minute window, the host is saturated and new builds will keep waiting. That is a capacity problem, not necessarily a crash: the machine is still up, but throughput drops and timeouts become more likely until load falls or more cores are added.

The date command printed Sat Oct 3 04:43:36 PM EDT 2026. That string is the system clock’s local time at the moment the command ran, formatted as weekday, month, day, clock time, meridian, timezone abbreviation, and year. EDT means Eastern Daylight Time, which is four hours behind UTC, so the same instant would be 20:43:36 UTC. The shell returned that line with exit code 0, which means the command completed normally and simply reported the clock rather than changing it.

Server clocks drift because the hardware that keeps time is not perfect. Typical machines use a quartz crystal oscillator whose frequency shifts with temperature, voltage, age, and manufacturing tolerance, so a few seconds of error can accumulate over days if nothing corrects it. Virtual machines add more error because the guest clock can stall or jump when the hypervisor pauses the VM or when the host itself is under load. Network time protocols such as NTP or chrony periodically compare the local clock to reference servers and slew or step it back into line, but until the next correction the clock keeps walking away from true time.
